query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a compressive surface treatment such as shot peening to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will improve its load-bearing integrity by inducing beneficial compressive residual stresses at the surface, thereby reducing crack initiation and propagation without altering the phase transitions responsible for its caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric response but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a compressive surface treatment (shot peening) designed to induce a layer of compressive residual stress on the surface.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under operating refrigeration conditions, with relevant applied magnetic or pressure fields, at ambient to moderate temperatures and under mechanical load conditions typical of service during cyclic refrigeration operation.
generation.structural_mediator: An induced compressive stress layer and modest surface densification that mitigate tensile stress concentrations at the surface while leaving the bulk microstructure (and hence the order-disorder transitions driving the caloric effect) unaltered.
generation.mechanism: The shot peening produces compressive residual stresses at the surface, which counteract the applied tensile stresses during loading. This delays the initiation and propagation of surface cracks, thereby improving load-bearing capacity. Because the treatment is confined to the surface and does not change the bulk phase or the order-disorder transition, the caloric performance remains preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced mechanical integrity (i.e., increased resistance to crack initiation and improved fracture toughness) with unchanged caloric response (entropy and temperature change characteristics) relative to that of the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which exhibits a large caloric effect but poor load-bearing integrity and is prone to cracking under operating conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under the typical refrigeration operating regimes (applied-field and pressure-field cycling, moderate mechanical loads) encountered during use; efficacy under extreme loads or temperatures remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: Although compressive surface treatments are known to improve mechanical integrity in many alloys without affecting bulk thermodynamic properties, the direct impact on the caloric performance in this specific high-entropy alloy requires experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one group subjected to shot peening and one untreated control group. Under identical testing conditions, perform cyclic mechanical load tests combined with the application of the relevant fields (magnetic or pressure) used in the standard caloric cycle. Monitor both the evolution of surface cracks and mechanical properties (via fatigue and fracture toughness tests) and the caloric response (measuring entropy changes and temperature shifts during the applied-field/pressure cycles).
measurements: Residual stress profiles (by X-ray diffraction or similar techniques)
Fatigue life and fracture toughness metrics
Caloric effect parameters (temperature change and entropy change during cycling)
Microstructural evaluation (to check for any treatment-induced bulk changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the shot-peened samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in load-bearing integrity (delayed crack formation or increased fracture toughness) or if their caloric response is significantly degraded relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The sliding wear test demonstrates a significant correlation between the applied stress and the rate of wear, as illustrated in Fig. 3a–e. Wear rate of the Cu matrix and surface composites augmented with high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibits a significant rise as the applied load is increased. The figure demonstrates a discernible connection between the wear rate and load, indicating that the wear rate exhibits a positive correlation with increasing load increments. The observed correlation between the increasing load and the accelerated rate of wear in case of composite and copper matrix suggests a corresponding increase in material loss under higher loads. This increase in material loss is due to increased plastic deformation induced at the higher loading conditions during sliding. This increase in plastic deformation results in material transfer between the sliding parts, from soft material to hard material which will come out as debris. This loss of material due to plastic deformation increases higher load and hence wear rate increases.
